Conjoint experiments show each respondent several randomly generated profiles and ask
them to choose between them. The usual estimand is the **average marginal component
effect (AMCE)**: the change in the probability that a profile is chosen when one attribute
moves from its baseline level to another level. Under randomization, AMCEs are the
coefficients of a linear probability model. Each respondent answers several tasks, so
standard errors are clustered by respondent.

Conjoint surveys are fielded in waves and watched as responses arrive. Re-checking
ordinary clustered p-values at every look inflates the false positive rate. `avlm` gives
the same regression with **cluster-robust confidence sequences and anytime-valid
p-values** (Lindon, 2026). You can look after every respondent and stop as soon as the
answer is clear.

## The data

Bansak, Hainmueller and Hangartner (2016) asked 18,000 Europeans in 15 countries to choose
between pairs of hypothetical asylum seekers, five pairs each. Each profile varied nine
attributes. Here we use three of them: occupation, religion and the reason for migrating.
The data are in the [Item Response Warehouse](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/conjoint_standard.html):


```r
library(irw)
d <- irw_fetch("bansak_2016_asylum", source = "conj")
d$attr_occupation <- relevel(factor(d$attr_occupation), "Unemployed")
d$attr_religion   <- relevel(factor(d$attr_religion), "Christian")
d$attr_reason     <- relevel(factor(d$attr_reason), "Persecution for political views")
```

Each respondent contributes ten rows, one per profile, and `choice` records which profile of
each pair they picked:


```r
r1 <- d[d$id == 1, c("task", "profile", "choice", "attr_occupation", "attr_religion",
                     "attr_reason", "cov_survey_weight")]
r1[order(r1$task, r1$profile), ]
```

## The standard analysis, and the avlm version

The usual analysis is a weighted linear probability model with standard errors clustered
by respondent:


```r
library(sandwich)
fit <- lm(choice ~ attr_occupation + attr_religion + attr_reason, data = d,
          weights = pmin(cov_survey_weight, 6))
se <- sqrt(diag(vcovCL(fit, cluster = ~id)))
round(cbind(AMCE = coef(fit), SE = se), 3)
#>                                                    AMCE    SE
#> (Intercept)                                       0.514 0.005
#> attr_occupationAccountant                         0.079 0.005
#> attr_occupationCleaner                            0.047 0.005
#> attr_occupationDoctor                             0.133 0.005
#> attr_occupationFarmer                             0.056 0.005
#> attr_occupationTeacher                            0.092 0.005
#> attr_religionAgnostic                            -0.036 0.004
#> attr_religionMuslim                              -0.107 0.004
#> attr_reasonPersecution for ethnicity              0.009 0.004
#> attr_reasonPersecution for religious beliefs      0.006 0.004
#> attr_reasonSeeking better economic opportunities -0.151 0.004
```

These match the published estimates. Muslim applicants are about 11 points less likely to
be chosen than Christian ones, and economic migrants about 15 points less likely than people
fleeing political persecution.



The anytime-valid version uses the same fit and the same cluster formula:


```r
library(avlm)
afit <- av(fit, g = 2191, cluster = ~id)
summary(afit)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = choice ~ attr_occupation + attr_religion + attr_reason, 
#>     data = d, weights = pmin(cov_survey_weight, 6))

#>      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max
```

`summary()` keeps the `lm` layout. It reports CR1 cluster-robust standard errors, the number
of clusters, and anytime-valid p-values. The 147 respondents with a missing survey weight are
dropped by `lm()`, and `av()` drops their clusters too. The standard errors match
`vcovCL(fit, cluster = ~id, type = "HC0")` exactly:


```r
all.equal(sqrt(diag(vcov(afit))), sqrt(diag(vcovCL(fit, cluster = ~id, type = "HC0"))))
#> [1] TRUE
```

`confint()` gives the 95% confidence sequences. Here they are next to the Wald intervals:


```r
ci <- confint(afit)
tab <- data.frame(
  term = names(coef(fit))[-1],
  amce = coef(fit)[-1],
  wald_lo = (coef(fit) - qnorm(0.975) * se)[-1],
  wald_hi = (coef(fit) + qnorm(0.975) * se)[-1],
  av_lo = ci[-1, 1],
  av_hi = ci[-1, 2],
  av_p = coef(summary(afit))[-1, 4]
)
format(tab[, -1], digits = 2)
#>                                                     amce  wald_lo wald_hi
#> attr_occupationAccountant                         0.0786  0.06820   0.089
#> attr_occupationCleaner                            0.0470  0.03641   0.058

#> attr_occupationFarmer                             0.0565  0.04615   0.067
```

The anytime-valid intervals are wider than the Wald intervals. That width is what it costs
to be allowed to look at the data at any time:

## Watching the survey come in

Suppose the survey had been analysed while it was fielded, re-running the regression after
every 250 respondents. The data do not record the order in which people responded, so we
replay the respondents in a random order. The confidence sequences are valid
**simultaneously at every look**, so we can stop as soon as an AMCE is clearly different
from zero. With Wald intervals that is not allowed, as the next section shows.


```r
set.seed(2016)
arrival <- sample(unique(d$id))
d$arrival <- match(d$id, arrival)

looks <- seq(250, length(arrival), by = 250)
terms <- c("attr_reasonSeeking better economic opportunities", "attr_religionMuslim",
           "attr_religionAgnostic", "attr_reasonPersecution for ethnicity")

path <- do.call(rbind, lapply(looks, function(n_resp) {
  fit_n <- lm(choice ~ attr_occupation + attr_religion + attr_reason,
              data = d[d$arrival <= n_resp, ], weights = pmin(cov_survey_weight, 6))
  ci_n <- confint(av(fit_n, g = 2191, cluster = ~id), parm = terms)
  se_n <- sqrt(diag(vcovCL(fit_n, cluster = ~id)))[terms]
  data.frame(respondents = n_resp, term = terms, est = coef(fit_n)[terms],
             av_lo = ci_n[, 1], av_hi = ci_n[, 2],
             wald_lo = coef(fit_n)[terms] - qnorm(0.975) * se_n,
             wald_hi = coef(fit_n)[terms] + qnorm(0.975) * se_n)
}))

# first look at which each confidence sequence excludes zero
settled_at <- sapply(split(path, path$term), function(p) {
  p$respondents[which(p$av_hi < 0 | p$av_lo > 0)[1]]
})
settled_at[terms]
#> attr_reasonSeeking better economic opportunities 
#>                                              500 
#>                              attr_religionMuslim 
#>                                              750 
#>                            attr_religionAgnostic 
#>                                             2750 
#>             attr_reasonPersecution for ethnicity 
#>                                               NA
```

<div class="figure">
<img src="conjoint-monitor-plot-1.png" alt="Confidence sequences for four AMCEs narrowing as respondents arrive, with the point where each first excludes zero marked." width="100%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk monitor-plot</p>
</div>

The penalty for economic migrants and the penalty for Muslim applicants are settled with a
small fraction of the 18,000 respondents. The Agnostic penalty takes longer. The difference
between ethnic and political persecution is close to zero and is never declared different
from zero, however long you watch.

## Why not just peek at the clustered Wald p-values?

To see what goes wrong, add a **placebo attribute** to the real data: a random label,
"A" or "B", given to each profile independently of everything else. Its true AMCE is zero by
construction, and the real respondents' choices keep their real within-respondent
correlation. We look after every 100 respondents up to 2,000 and record when each test first
rejects at the 5% level:


```r
set.seed(1)
reps <- 500
looks_null <- seq(100, 2000, by = 100)

rejected <- replicate(reps, {
  first <- sample(unique(d$id), 2000)
  d0 <- d[d$id %in% first, ]
  d0$arrival <- match(d0$id, first)
  d0$placebo <- factor(sample(c("A", "B"), nrow(d0), replace = TRUE))
  sapply(looks_null, function(n_resp) {
    fit0 <- lm(choice ~ placebo, data = d0[d0$arrival <= n_resp, ],
               weights = pmin(cov_survey_weight, 6))
    afit0 <- av(fit0, g = 2191, cluster = ~id)
    z <- coef(fit0)[["placeboB"]] / sqrt(vcov(afit0)["placeboB", "placeboB"])
    c(wald = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)) < 0.05,
      avlm = coef(summary(afit0))["placeboB", 4] < 0.05)
  })
})
# rejected[test, look, rep]; has a test rejected at this look or any earlier one?
ever <- apply(rejected, c(1, 3), cummax)
false_positive_rate <- apply(ever, c(1, 2), mean)
false_positive_rate[nrow(false_positive_rate), ]
#>  wald  avlm 
#> 0.236 0.000
```

Checking the clustered Wald test 20 times gives a false positive rate several times the
promised 5%. The anytime-valid test stays below 5% however often you look.

## Notes

* `av(fit, cluster = ~id)` takes a one-sided formula, a column name (`"id"`), or a vector of
  ids. Weights, `subset` and missing values are handled the same way as in `lm()`.
* The cluster-robust e-values and confidence sequences, with their exact and asymptotic
  guarantees, are developed in Lindon (2026),
  [arXiv:2610.25613](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25613).

### References

Bansak, K., Hainmueller, J. and Hangartner, D. (2016). How economic, humanitarian, and
religious concerns shape European attitudes toward asylum seekers. *Science*, 354(6309),
217–222.

Lindon, M. (2026). Anytime-Valid Inference in Linear Models with Clustered Outcomes: Exact
Multivariate Tests and Cluster-Robust Confidence Sequences. arXiv:2610.25613.
